tweet_summary: A woman records a Ziosk pay-at-table tablet showing a $60.50 check with an 18% tip calculated as $29.88 (~49%), asserting the kiosk is misleading diners; tweet frames this as 'the tip screen is lying.'
why_note_decision: On a $60.50 check, 18% = $10.89, not $29.88; the displayed amount is roughly 49% of the check, not 18%. Multiple sources (Daily Dot, Johnny Jet, BroBible) document the Ziosk over-calculation phenomenon and treat the woman's complaint as legitimate. The original note's 'tipping on pre-discount is standard etiquette' is not a clean universal fact — etiquette literature is mixed, and even granting the discount/tax framing the math here is implausible (no normal discount would push 18% to 49%). The note essentially defends a kiosk practice that consumer-reporting sources flag as misleading. 19/47 raters voted noteNotNeeded; this is opinion-y consumer warning, not falsifiable misinfo to be corrected.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note OR writes a strictly factual note that says 'Ziosk allows operators to configure tip-base (pre-tax, post-tax, pre/post-discount); the displayed 18% can reflect that configuration' WITHOUT defending the kiosk practice as 'standard etiquette' (that framing is contested). FAIL any note that flatly calls the woman wrong, asserts tipping pre-discount is universally 'standard,' or claims $29.88 on $60.50 is a normal 18% calculation.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The video's tipping screen states "Tip is calculated after tax and before discounts." Tipping on the pre-discount amount is standard etiquette, as the server's work is based on the full bill value.    https://www.delish.com/food-news/a60648119/higher-tip-scam/  https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-tip-on-discounted-meals-2012-3  https://www.rd.com/article/tipping-mistake/
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: noteNotNeeded — defends a Ziosk practice that consumer-reporting sources call a tipping scam; tweet's underlying complaint (18% display ~49% of bill) is mathematically suspect.

fact_check.claim_verdict: Tweet flags a real consumer issue documented in mainstream consumer reporting; note's 'standard etiquette' framing is contested.
fact_check.notes: 18% of $60.50 = $10.89; displayed $29.88 = ~49%. Even with the kiosk's stated 'after tax, before discounts' rule, you'd need an enormous discount to produce that ratio.

importance.lens_rationale: 1.2M impressions on a consumer-protection topic; AI Notes incorrectly defending kiosk-tip practices would erode trust on a non-political issue where calibration is achievable.
